name: Zero Revenue Generated
subject: quantum-computing
subjectTitle: A Skeptic's Guide to Quantum Computing

lesson.title: The Revenue Line Nobody Wants Next to the Investment Line
lesson.summary: Setting the tens of billions in already-spent quantum computing capital against the commercial revenue produced so far yields an uncomfortable ratio, though literal zero slightly overstates a genuinely small but real number.
lesson.body:
The previous chapter separated the "$100 billion" headline into layers: tens of billions already spent, private capital plus disbursed government funding, versus a much larger pool of pledges aimed at the 2030s. This chapter asks the obvious next question: what has the already-spent tens of billions actually produced in commercial revenue? The honest answer is not literally zero, but it is small enough relative to the capital deployed that "zero" works as a meaningful rhetorical shorthand rather than a wild exaggeration.

The handful of publicly traded, pure-play quantum computing companies, hardware and software vendors that disclose financial results because they trade on public markets, collectively report annual revenues in the tens of millions of dollars, not hundreds of millions, and nowhere near billions. Set beside a sector that has absorbed tens of billions in cumulative investment, the industry-wide revenue-to-invested-capital ratio is, by any reasonable estimate, well under one percent per year. For comparison, recall the opportunity-cost chapter's index fund: the same tens of billions of dollars parked in a diversified index fund earning a historically typical 8 to 9 percent annually would generate more cash return in a single year than the entire quantum computing industry currently generates in commercial revenue.

The gap is not really a mystery, and it connects directly back to net present value. Most invested capital has gone toward basic hardware research, error-correction work, and talent, spending whose payoff, if it arrives, was always modeled for the 2030s and beyond, not the mid-2020s. Today's revenue comes mostly from cloud access fees for running experiments on current, pre-fault-tolerant machines, consulting and pilot engagements, and government research contracts, valuable for keeping companies alive and learning, but categorically different from the large-scale commercial workloads, drug discovery, materials science, logistics optimization at production scale, that the original investment thesis was built around.

The skeptic's honest framing is not "quantum computing has generated zero revenue, therefore it is a scam." That overstates the case and ignores real, if modest, commercial activity. It is closer to this: the industry is roughly two decades into a commercialization arc, and the technology S-curve analysis from the probability-of-success chapter would place a comparably fundamental, hardware-first computing technology's own historical path at two to four decades long. A revenue-to-investment ratio this low is disappointing relative to the hype, but it is not obviously anomalous relative to the historical base rate for transformative computing technologies.

What should actually concern a rational investor is not the tiny current revenue figure taken in isolation, it is whether the trend looks like an S-curve about to bend upward or a flat line with no visible inflection point yet. A revenue-to-investment ratio that stays near zero for another five to eight years, even amid ever-larger funding rounds, the subject of the next chapter, would be a far stronger signal that the underlying thesis is broken than today's still-early-days number is on its own.
